newsitem.title: ISRAEL: One killed in Israel stadium bridge collapse.
newsitem.headline: One killed in Israel stadium bridge collapse.

text.p: A bridge at an Israeli sports stadium collapsed on Monday minutes before the opening parade of an international Jewish sporting event, killing one person and injuring 34, police said.

Members of the 370-strong Australian team were standing on the pedestrian bridge over the Yarkon River ready to enter the Ramat Gan Stadium near Tel Aviv for the quadrennial Maccabiah Games nicknamed the "Jewish Olympics".

Police said one person was killed and 34 injured, three of them seriously, when the wooden bridge supported by metal bars collapsed in the middle. Israel Radio said the dead man was apparently an Australian in his 50s or 60s who drowned.
Two rescue workers were also injured.

Israel Television showed a bag with a body in it. Other television pictures showed a clustre of youngsters in muddied white sports uniforms crammed into the crack of the bridge at the point where it fell into the water.
Organisers cancelled the march of national teams but went ahead with the opening ceremonies for the games which bring together Jewish athletes from all over the world.
An hour and 40 minutes later, following a torch-lighting ceremony, organisers informed the crowd of tens of thousands of the disaster and ended the ceremony.
It was not immediately clear what caused the bridge to collapse. There was no immediate suggestion of foul play.
Louis Platus, head of the Australian delegation, told Reuters: "About 100 of us were on the bridge. We were on the bridge when it collapsed at our feet."
He said some of the delegation's rugby players jumped in the water to pull people from the water.

"We were walking across. All of a sudden we heard a bang," Harry Purcell, the Australia team manager, told reporters. "And then all of a sudden in slow motion it just collapsed in the middle and we started to slide."

One of the Australian delegation members, Ari Kochmalik, told Israel Television: "I was on the bridge. There were a lot of people on the bridge and the bridge fell. That's what happened. And there was water under the bridge and there are a number of people who fell in the water.
"I fell in the water and suddenly I felt air, thank God, but I don't know what happened to the other people," he said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attended the opening ceremonies. He left a short time later to visit the wounded in hospital.

The television broadcast pictures of Netanyahu's security men scrambling amidst ambulances rushing to help wounded when the bridge collapsed. Ambulances carried away wounded while stunned spectators watched from the packed stadium.
A wet, shoeless and shirtless Australian named Zorek, a 15-year-old tennis player, told reporters he wasn't hurt but described what he said was the worst experience of his life.
"I was under the water. I thought I was going to die. My head was under the water. I couldn't breathe for a minute until I felt the ground."
"There were a lot of people around me. I thought I was going to die. This is the worst thing that's ever happened to me."
"I just saw a few chess players and tenpin bowling people that were injured and I couldn't breathe and they were all pale and that's all I knew," he said.
Some 40 minutes after the collapse of the bridge, while rescuers formed human chains and marched into the marshy waters, Israeli President Ezer Weizman declared the games open.
"I am sorry this is the way to open the Maccabiah which should be more joyous and I hope that in this Maccabiah that there will be accomplishments that will make all of us happy," he told the crowd.

As rescue efforts continued, the crowd saw a programme featuring a three-dimensional laser-created hologram of a Star of David along with a memorial ceremony to the victims of the Nazi Holocaust and the fallen of Israel's wars and guerrilla attacks followed by a song-and-dance show.
